title: Interfaces
summary: Master pure specification contracts in Java: the interface keyword, implicit public abstract methods, public static final constants, and 100% abstraction.
learningObjectives: Define Java interfaces as pure behavioral contracts specifying what methods a class must support
Identify compiler implicits: all interface methods are implicitly public abstract (prior to Java 8)
Explain constant rules: all interface variables are implicitly public static final
Compare interface design (CAN-DO capabilities) with class inheritance (IS-A identity)
expectedOutcomes: You can declare clean interfaces with method specifications and constants
You understand why interfaces represent 100% pure contracts without instance state

activities.title: Practical Context: Standardized Contracts Across Unrelated Classes
activities.concept: The Interface as a Universal Socket

realWorldMetaphor.scenario: A USB-C port is a standardized specification: it defines exact pin dimensions, voltage profiles (5V, 9V, 20V), and protocol handshakes. An iPhone, a high-end laptop, an external SSD, a drone battery charger, and a desk fan all have USB-C ports. A laptop and a desk fan share almost zero DNA (they are not in the same class hierarchy), yet both plug into the same charger.
realWorldMetaphor.mapping: The USB-C specification is the `interface` (`Chargeable`). The phone, SSD, and desk fan are completely unrelated classes that implement the same interface (`implements Chargeable`). The charger interacts strictly with the `Chargeable` contract.
realWorldMetaphor.takeaway: Interfaces enable polymorphic interaction across completely unrelated classes based on shared capabilities, not shared ancestry.

activities.content:
In modular software systems, unrelated classes across different parts of the application must frequently support a common capability.

For example, a `User` entity, a `DatabaseBackup` task, and a `ServerConfiguration` file may all need to be written to disk as JSON.

An interface establishes a universal contract that any class can implement regardless of where it sits in the class inheritance tree.

questions.question: What modifiers are automatically added by the Java compiler to every variable declared in an interface?
questions.explanation: All interface variables are implicitly `public`, `static`, and `final`. They are compile-time constants.

questions.question: What modifiers are automatically added by the compiler to a standard method header `void run();` declared in an interface?
questions.explanation: All non-default, non-static interface methods are implicitly `public` and `abstract`.

questions.question: Can an interface have a constructor in Java?
options: Yes, a default no-arg constructor only
No, interfaces cannot have constructors because they cannot hold instance state and cannot be directly instantiated
questions.explanation: Interfaces have no instance fields and cannot be instantiated, so constructors are completely disallowed.

questions.question: Can you declare a method in an interface with `protected` access?
options: Yes, protected is the default access modifier in interfaces
No, interface methods cannot be protected; they are strictly public (or private helper methods in Java 9+)
Only if the interface is in the java.util package
Yes, if the interface is package-private
questions.explanation: Interface methods represent public contracts. `protected` interface methods cause a compile-time error: 'modifier protected not allowed here'.

questions.question: What happens if you attempt `interface A { int count; }` without initializing `count`?
options: Compile error: variable count might not have been initialized (interface fields are final)
questions.explanation: Because interface fields are implicitly `final`, they MUST be assigned an explicit initial value at declaration time.

questions.question: What keyword is used by a class to adopt an interface?
questions.explanation: Classes use the `implements` keyword to establish a contract with one or more interfaces.

questions.question: Can an interface extend another interface in Java?
options: No, interfaces can only be implemented by classes
Yes, an interface can extend one or more other interfaces using the extends keyword
Only if both interfaces are empty
questions.explanation: An interface can extend other interfaces using `extends` (e.g. `interface B extends A`), inheriting all methods and constants.

questions.question: Can you instantiate an interface directly: `Runnable r = new Runnable();`?
options: No, compile error: Runnable is abstract; cannot be instantiated
questions.explanation: Interfaces cannot be instantiated directly with `new Interface()`. An implementing class or anonymous class must provide the bodies.

questions.question: Why are interfaces said to model 'CAN-DO' relationships rather than 'IS-A' relationships?
options: Because CAN-DO is faster at runtime
Because an interface specifies a capability (e.g., Serializable, Comparable, Printable) that completely unrelated classes can acquire
questions.explanation: Class inheritance models identity ('Sparrow IS-A Bird'). Interfaces model cross-cutting capabilities ('Airplane CAN-DO Fly', 'Sparrow CAN-DO Fly').

questions.question: What is a marker (tagging) interface in Java?
options: An interface with 10 or more methods
An interface with zero fields and zero methods, used to mark a class as possessing a certain property (e.g., Serializable, Cloneable)
An interface that can only be used by the JVM internally
questions.explanation: A marker interface has no methods or fields (e.g. `java.io.Serializable`); it tags a class for metadata checks via `instanceof`.

interviewQA.question: Why are all fields in a Java interface automatically `public static final`?
interviewQA.answer: An interface is a pure behavioral specification, not an implementation of state. Allowing non-static instance fields would introduce object state into interfaces, creating multiple inheritance of state with all its associated memory ambiguity and diamond problem collisions. Making all fields `public static final` ensures they are strictly immutable compile-time constants.

interviewQA.question: Can an interface extend multiple interfaces simultaneously? Why does Java permit this while forbidding multiple class inheritance?
interviewQA.answer: Yes, an interface can extend multiple interfaces: `interface C extends A, B`. Java permits this because interfaces inherit only method specifications (or signatures), not instance state or method bodies (traditionally). There is no ambiguity regarding state layout in heap memory, so multiple interface inheritance does not suffer from the classic Diamond Problem of multiple class inheritance.

interviewQA.question: What is a Marker Interface, and why have modern Java architectures largely replaced them with Annotations?
interviewQA.answer: A Marker Interface (e.g. `Serializable`, `Cloneable`, `Remote`) contains zero methods and zero constants, serving solely as a type tag checked via `instanceof`. Modern Java prefers Annotations (e.g. `@Entity`, `@Test`) because annotations can carry parameterized metadata, can target fields/methods/classes, and avoid polluting the type hierarchy.

interviewQA.question: Why does a class implementing an interface have to declare its overriding methods as `public`?
interviewQA.answer: Methods in an interface are implicitly `public`. In Java, an overriding method in a subclass cannot reduce the visibility of the method it overrides. Therefore, any class implementing an interface method must explicitly declare the method as `public`; omitting `public` causes a compiler error: 'cannot reduce the visibility of the inherited method from Interface'.

interviewQA.question: How do interfaces enable Dependency Injection (DI) and Unit Testing?
interviewQA.answer: When a business service depends on an interface (e.g., `PaymentGateway`) rather than a concrete class (`StripeGateway`), developers can inject mock implementations (`MockPaymentGateway`) during unit tests. This isolates the service under test from real external network I/O, speeding up tests and making them 100% deterministic.

interviewQA.question: What bytecode instruction is generated when calling a method on an interface reference?
interviewQA.answer: The JVM generates the `invokeinterface` instruction. At runtime, the JVM looks up the interface table (itable) associated with the actual runtime class to find the target method offset, which has slightly different lookup semantics than `invokevirtual`.

activities.title: Self-Evaluation Checklist
checklist: I know the exact syntax for declaring an interface using the interface keyword.
I understand that all interface variables are implicitly public static final.
I understand that all standard interface methods are implicitly public abstract.
I know why interfaces cannot have constructors.
I understand that an interface can extend multiple other interfaces using extends.
I know why implementing classes must declare overridden methods as public.
I can explain the difference between CAN-DO (interfaces) and IS-A (classes).
I understand what marker interfaces are (e.g. Serializable).
I know how interfaces enable dependency injection and mock testing.
I can process heterogeneous objects through a shared interface reference.

practiceProblems.title: Data Encryption Capability Interface
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build an encryption interface from scratch:

1. Interface Encryptor:
   - Method: String encrypt(String plainText);

2. Implementing Classes:
   - Class Rot13Encryptor: @Override public String encrypt(String text) returning '[ROT13] ' + text
   - Class Base64MockEncryptor: @Override public String encrypt(String text) returning '[B64] ' + text

Test in Main:
Encryptor enc1 = new Rot13Encryptor(); print enc1.encrypt("HelloWorld");
Encryptor enc2 = new Base64MockEncryptor(); print enc2.encrypt("HelloWorld");.
hints: Implement encrypt(String plainText) as public in both classes.
Loop over Encryptor[] suite and print e.encrypt(sample).
practiceProblems.description: Create an Encryptor interface and implement Rot13 and Base64 encryption from scratch.

practiceProblems.title: Fix Package-Private Visibility in Interface Implementation
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Fix compiler error: 'cannot reduce the visibility of the inherited method':

Bug: In MemoryCache, methods `put()` and `get()` were written without `public`. In Java, interface methods are ALWAYS public, so implementing methods cannot be package-private!

Your Task:
1. In MemoryCache, add the `public` modifier to `void put(String key, String value)` and `String get(String key)`.
2. Add `@Override` above both methods.

Test in Main:
Cache cache = new MemoryCache();
cache.put("token", "xyz123");
Print 'Cached: ' + cache.get("token");.
hints: Add public to both put and get in MemoryCache.
practiceProblems.description: All methods declared in an interface are implicitly public. Implementing methods MUST be declared public.
